title: Social Security Recipients Could See Larger Benefit Boost in 2027, Fox Business Reports
body:
A new set of estimates released this week suggests that Social Security recipients could see their 2027 cost‑of‑living adjustment (COLA) rise to somewhere between 3.4 % and 3.6 %, a noticeable jump from the 2.8 % increase applied for 2026. The projected boost reflects the latest data on consumer‑price inflation and will be finalized after the September CPI report is published later this month.

The Social Security Administration (SSA) typically bases the annual COLA on the percentage change in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI‑UW) over the 12‑month period ending in the third month of the preceding year. For the 2026 adjustment, the SSA used the CPI data from the third quarter of 2024, which showed a 2.8 % rise in prices. Analysts now expect that the CPI for the third quarter of 2025 will be higher, pushing the COLA into the mid‑3 % range. While the exact figure will not be confirmed until the September CPI release, the range of 3.4 %–3.6 % has already been floated by the agency’s internal projections.

The anticipated increase could have a meaningful impact on the roughly 66 million Americans who receive Social Security benefits, many of whom rely on the program as their primary source of income. A 3.5 % boost translates into an additional $70 to $120 per month for most retirees, with larger gains for those receiving higher benefit amounts. For seniors on fixed incomes, even modest improvements in purchasing power can help offset rising costs for essentials such as healthcare, housing, and groceries.

Economists note that the projected COLA aligns with broader inflation trends that have persisted despite the Federal Reserve’s aggressive rate‑hiking cycle. While headline inflation has moderated from its post‑pandemic peak, core price pressures—particularly in housing, medical care, and energy—remain elevated. The SSA’s methodology, which captures price changes across a wide basket of goods and services, tends to produce adjustments that lag the broader economy by several months. Consequently, the 2027 COLA will likely reflect inflation that was already evident in the summer of 2025.

Policy makers are also watching the numbers closely because higher COLAs increase the program’s outlay. Social Security’s trust funds, which are projected to be depleted by the mid‑2030s under current law, could face added strain if inflation continues to outpace wage growth. Some legislators have floated proposals to cap future COLAs or to tie them to wage growth instead of price indices, arguing that such changes would preserve the program’s solvency. However, consumer advocates warn that limiting adjustments would erode the purchasing power of seniors, especially those without supplemental retirement savings.

Looking ahead, the final COLA figure will be announced in early October, once the September CPI data are released. If the estimate holds, beneficiaries can anticipate a modest but welcome increase that outpaces the previous year’s adjustment. The move underscores the delicate balance the SSA must strike between protecting retirees from inflation and managing the long‑term fiscal health of the nation’s largest social insurance program. As inflation dynamics evolve, the next round of adjustments will remain a focal point for retirees, policymakers, and financial planners alike.
